title: Blink and You Lose
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Timed to the release of The Boys in the Boat, this piece uses competitive rowing as a metaphor for the discipline of undistracted focus. The author argues that any lapse in attention, however small, breaks the synchrony that elite teams need to perform, and that the same principle applies well beyond athletics. The piece specifically warns against leaders and teams who focus outward on competitors rather than inward on their own execution, framing distraction-free focus as a defining trait of excellence.
points: Even a small, momentary shift in focus — like a rower glancing at a competing boat — can destroy the synchrony a high-performing team depends on.
True excellence in nearly any discipline requires a disciplined, unwavering focus void of distraction, not just talent.
Teams that turn their attention outward toward competitors, instead of inward toward their own execution, undermine their own performance.
The film's central lesson is that the most exceptional performer is often simply the average person sustaining a laser-like focus.
quotes: The film offers a myriad of life lessons, but also provides the ideal backdrop from which to understand the beauty of teamwork.
Any shift in focus and the fluidity of the rowing performance becomes interrupted to the detriment of the boat.
If any team member so much as makes a darting glance at the crew next to them to see which boat is ahead, they destroy the synchrony necessary to win.
This is especially true when leaders and teams turn their attention outward toward competitors, instead of inward toward execution and performance.
We learn that the most exceptional performer is always the average person with a laser-like focus.
